title: Interfaith families
hookLine: some Jews live in interfaith families, and communities respond in different ways

cards: A couple sits at a kitchen table with a notebook, planning a wedding. One of them is Jewish; the other isn't. The guest list is easy.
The menu is easy. Then come the questions nobody wants to say out loud. Who will marry us?
Under a chuppah, or not? And later, quietly: if we have children, what will they be? Their two families listen from a distance, hoping, worrying, loving them both.
Jewish communities have been asked this for a long time, and they don't all give the same answer.

teach.b: The Torah itself holds more than one view. Moses marries Zipporah, the daughter of Jethro, a priest of Midian.

Later Jethro watches Moses judging the people from morning until evening, alone, worn down, and tells him to share the load: "So Moses hearkened to the voice of his father-in-law, and did all that he had said."
The great lawgiver takes advice from a priest of another people.

But the same Torah warns against marrying into the nations of Canaan, for fear the children will be turned away from God. And in the book of Ezra, returning exiles are told to send away foreign wives.
The Bible doesn't settle it in one verse.

teach.h: STATUS THROUGH THE MOTHER, OR EITHER PARENT.
teach.b: The rabbis then made a rule about children: in the Mishnah, a child's Jewish status follows the mother. That rule still shapes communities, and they respond in different ways.
Orthodox communities hold to traditional Jewish law: their rabbis don't officiate at interfaith weddings, and the child of a Jewish mother is Jewish.
Conservative communities also follow the mother's line, and some reach out warmly to interfaith families who come through the door.

Reform and Reconstructionist communities in North America accept a child with one Jewish parent, mother or father, who is raised as a Jew, and some of their rabbis officiate at interfaith weddings while others don't.
Each holds its position for reasons it cares about: continuity, law, welcome, love.
Meanwhile, real families live it. A non-Jewish parent drives the kids to Hebrew school every week. Grandparents learn new holidays.
A child carries two sets of stories.

how: Jewish communities respond to interfaith families in different ways: Orthodox and Conservative communities follow descent through the mother and their rabbis generally do not officiate at interfaith weddings, while Reform and Reconstructionist communities accept a child of either Jewish parent raised as a Jew, and some of their rabbis officiate.

games.q: you're Moses, judging the people alone from morning until evening. your father-in-law, a priest of Midian, says you'll wear yourself out. what do you do?
o: thank him, and keep doing it all yourself.
listen to him, and share the load as he says.
step down, and let someone else lead.
games.why: Moses listens, and does all that Jethro said. the great lawgiver takes advice from a priest of another people.

practice: Picture a family that holds more than one tradition, your own, a neighbor's or a friend's, gathered around their table on a holiday. Who feels at home there, and who might feel a little on the edge?
If you pray, you can hold that family in your own words; if not, simply wish them well, one by one.

wordCard.voice: Interfaith families. Households where Jewish and other traditions share one table, met by Jewish communities in different ways. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: family. In the Bible it can mean a whole clan.

carryVoice: Your line: families are complex. Every table can hold more than one story. See you tomorrow.
